intro: Orlando keeps more than 100,000 trees and names one of them its oldest, a live oak with a park of its own on Thornton Avenue, struck by lightning at least three times in the 1970s. The city puts the Big Tree at likely 350 to 400 years. In Loch Haven Park, The Mayor has broken limbs twice and still lets the rest hang to the ground. And in Thornton Park, near Lake Eola, the oak of Constitution Green was saved in 2015 when the land it stands on came up for sale.
meta_description: Three live oaks in Orlando: the Big Tree, the city's oldest at 350 to 400 years, The Mayor in Loch Haven Park, and the oak of Constitution Green.
question_meta: Orlando's oldest tree is the Big Tree, a live oak put at 350 to 400 years in its own park on Thornton Avenue. Where it stands, and two more oaks.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Orlando is the live oak in Big Tree Park on North Thornton Avenue, named the oldest of the city's more than 100,000 maintained trees by its parks department. The City of Orlando says it is likely between 350 and 400 years old, and a USA Today network report says more than 400. Neither figure comes from a ring count. Do not confuse it with Big Tree Park in Longwood, north of the city, whose Senator fell in 2012.
question_context: All three of Orlando's oaks here are on the city's own Significant Trees list, and all three ages are estimates. The Big Tree's 350 to 400 years is the city's figure. Its trunk is reported as thick as 8 feet, without saying whether across or around, and its limbs reach out more than 30 feet each side. The city put up a placard there in the 1920s and bought the land about 30 years later, and recently a Michigan nonprofit, the Archangel Ancient Tree Archive, took samples to clone it. The Mayor, in Loch Haven Park beside the Mennello Museum, is put at over 200 years by the city and more than 300 by a newspaper feature. It broke limbs in 1998 and 2008, and its information display claims it had reached a third of its height when the Constitution was ratified. The oak at Constitution Green in Thornton Park is the youngest, probably 125 to 175 years by the city's reckoning, and has a crown shaped by a tree that once stood opposite. All three are free to visit.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Orlando?
faq.a: The live oak in Big Tree Park on North Thornton Avenue. The city says it is likely 350 to 400 years old and calls it the oldest tree in Orlando; a newspaper report says more than 400. Neither comes from a ring count.

faq.q: Is Big Tree Park in Orlando the same as the one in Longwood?
faq.a: No. Orlando's Big Tree Park is a small city park on Thornton Avenue north of downtown. The Big Tree Park in Longwood is a different place, where the Senator fell in 2012 and Lady Liberty still stands.

faq.q: How was the Constitution Green oak saved?
faq.a: In 2015 the land it stands on was leased from a private family who wanted to sell. A public campaign followed, and the city announced it would save both the tree and the green.

faq.q: Where is The Mayor in Orlando?
faq.a: In Loch Haven Park, on the lawn beside the Mennello Museum of American Art, north of downtown. An information display stands near the tree, and entry to the park is free.

trees.name: The Big Tree

location.address: Big Tree Park, 930 N Thornton Avenue, Orlando, FL 32803

trees.story:
Orlando looks after more than 100,000 trees, and its parks department names this live oak as the oldest of them. The city's own estimate is likely 350 to 400 years. A USA Today network report goes further and says more than 400. Neither figure comes with a ring count, so the fair answer is a range.

The tree has done some living in that time. Lightning struck it at least three times in the 1970s. Its limbs still reach out more than 30 feet on each side, and the same report puts the trunk as thick as 8 feet, without saying whether that means across or around.

People noticed it early. The city put up a placard at the tree in the 1920s and about 30 years later bought the land and opened a park, which is why Big Tree Park on Thornton Avenue is essentially one oak and the ground beneath it. More recently the Archangel Ancient Tree Archive, a Michigan nonprofit, climbed it and took samples to clone it, and the city expects young copies of its oldest tree to come out of that work.

Do not mix it up with the other Big Tree Park, in Longwood, north of the city. That park's famous Senator fell in 2012, and its neighbour Lady Liberty still stands.

Entry is free. The park sits north of downtown, about ten minutes by car from Lake Eola, with LYNX buses on Orange Avenue and Virginia Drive nearby.

trees.name: The Mayor

location.address: Orlando Loch Haven Park, 777 E Princeton Street, Orlando, FL 32803 (beside the Mennello Museum of American Art)

trees.story:
The Mayor has its own information display, and the display thinks big. It says the Mayaca people were living in central Florida when this live oak was a sapling, and that the tree stood at about a third of its present height when the United States ratified its Constitution.

The dates underneath that are less settled than the sign suggests. The City of Orlando, which owns the park, says over 200 years. A USA Today network feature on the city's trees says more than 300, and one caption gives 1688. None of them shows how it was worked out, so the age is somewhere from two centuries upward. If anyone has dated it properly, we would like to hear.

What the city states plainly is that it is a survivor. The Mayor broke limbs in 1998 and again in 2008 and is still on the city's list of significant trees. The limbs it kept hang down to the ground on all sides.

It stands in Loch Haven Park, the cultural campus north of downtown, on the lawn beside the Mennello Museum of American Art. Our pin marks the museum rather than the trunk, and the latest word on the tree is the city's own listing, so if you go, tell us how it is doing. Entry is free. LYNX buses and the SunRail station at Florida Hospital Health Village are roughly ten to twenty minutes away on foot.

trees.verify_notes: City of Orlando (owner): 'Over 200 years old, "The Mayor", is a Live Oak at Loch Haven Park that has survived despite limb breaks in 2008 and 1998.' Timber tour feature (Yahoo/USA Today network, fetched): 'more than 300-year-old', 'limbs hanging to the ground on all sides', an information display near the tree says Mayaca people lived in Central Florida when it was a sapling and that at roughly a third of its present height (about 50 ft) the US Constitution was ratified. Ages conflict (200+ city vs 300+ feature; one caption gives 1688); recorded as a broad range, no basis. Pin approximate: Mennello Museum point (28.5700, -81.3673) from a listing, not the tree; the tree is beside the museum, location text 'center of this park' in a travel guide. lifecheck NONE at that point, and no dated post-2008 news item on the tree found, so alive rests on the city's current page: flagged. trees.name: Constitution Green Oak

location.address: Constitution Green, 300 S Summerlin Avenue (S Eola Drive), Orlando, FL 32801

trees.story:
The only sure way to learn this oak's age, experts told a local news station in 2015, would be to cut it down. Orlando chose to keep the question open.

That was the year the tree nearly lost its ground. Constitution Green, a small lawn in Thornton Park a few minutes from Lake Eola, was leased from a private family who wanted to sell, and the oak at its centre was on the city's list of significant trees. A public campaign followed, and the city announced it would save both the tree and the park.

So the age stays an estimate. The city says probably 125 to 175 years, and Central Florida Public Media reported it as 175 by some estimates. That makes it young beside Orlando's oldest oaks. The reason to come is the shape.

On one side its branches lean out and come down to rest on the grass. The city explains why. Another tree once stood opposite, and the oak grew its crown away from it, so what you see now is the outline of a neighbour that is no longer there.

The green is free and open, an easy walk from Lake Eola Park, with LYNX downtown routes close by. Our pin marks the middle of the green rather than the trunk, and the oak stands near its centre.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the branches on one side that lean out and rest on the ground, a crown shaped by a tree that once stood opposite. It is the big live oak near the centre of Constitution Green in Thornton Park.

ClickOrlando 2015: city to save the tree and park, 'somewhere between 125 to 175 years old and experts say the only way to know how old it really is is to cut it down'; limbs reach the ground.
